# Building Your Data Science Portfolio

## Overview
Skills only get you hired if others can see them, and a portfolio is how a beginner data scientist proves capability without prior job experience. A strong portfolio isn't a pile of tutorials redone; it's a small set of two to four polished projects that each tell a clear story: a real problem, your approach, and a concrete result, ideally with at least one deployed app (like your capstone) that a recruiter can click and use. For each project you write a clear README or case study that frames the business question, summarizes your method, highlights key findings with a visual or two, and links to the live demo, because hiring managers skim and need the value in seconds. Your GitHub profile becomes your professional home: pin your best repositories, keep commit histories clean, and write a profile README introducing yourself. Optionally, writing short blog posts about your projects or participating in Kaggle demonstrates communication skills and initiative. The goal is that within a few minutes, anyone can see that you can take a problem from raw data all the way to a working, well-communicated solution, which is exactly what employers want to verify.

## Deep Dive
This module covers: What makes a strong DS portfolio; Choosing and framing portfolio projects; Writing project READMEs and case studies; GitHub profile and personal branding; Optional: blogging and Kaggle presence. Mastering these ideas is essential because they appear repeatedly in production AI systems.

### What You Will Learn
- The core theory behind today's topic.
- How to apply it using Python, NumPy, Pandas, or the relevant framework.
- How to evaluate results and avoid common mistakes.
- Where to find authoritative references when you need deeper detail.

### Real-World Context
In industry, these skills are used daily: data scientists clean messy survey data, AI engineers deploy models to REST APIs, and automation engineers orchestrate pipelines. Today's practical task simulates one of these real-world scenarios.

## Hands-On Practice
Practical Task: Curate your best two to four projects into a portfolio: write or improve each README as a mini case study, pin them on GitHub, and create a profile README introducing yourself and your skills.
Mini Project: Build a simple personal portfolio (a GitHub profile README or a lightweight portfolio site) that showcases your projects with descriptions, visuals, and links to live demos.
Assignment: Write a one-paragraph case study for your capstone suitable for the top of its README, framing the problem, approach, and result for a recruiter.

Complete all three sections. Each completed section earns points toward your CalibiAI Score. If you are unsure about any part, use the AI assessment popup to submit your work and receive dynamic feedback from DeepSeek.

## Common Mistakes to Avoid
Many beginners rush into coding before fully understanding the data. Others skip validation steps and overestimate model performance. This module helps you build the discipline of checking assumptions first, then applying algorithms systematically.

## Career Impact
The skills covered today are frequently tested in technical interviews and required in entry-level AI engineering roles. Building a portfolio that demonstrates mastery of these concepts will significantly improve your job prospects.

## Key Takeaways
1. Theory guides practice — understand before coding.
2. Clean data and clear metrics are more valuable than complex models.
3. Document your steps for reproducibility.
4. Communication matters: explain results to non-technical stakeholders.

## Next Steps After Today
- Complete the practical task and submit it for AI review.
- Read any research papers linked for deeper theory.
- Prepare questions for tomorrow's module.

## Resources
- Use the linked videos and documentation as reference material.
- Read the research papers for theoretical depth.
- Check the GitHub repositories for working code examples.
